reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: An invasive mycosis caused by the dimorphic fungus Talaromyces marneffei, endemic to South-East Asia, southern China and parts of north-eastern India
It occurs predominantly in people with advanced HIV and low CD4 counts, and is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection in endemic regions
Typical features are fever, weight loss, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and characteristic umbilicated, molluscum-like skin papules often on the face and trunk
Exposure to bamboo rats and their habitats is epidemiologically linked, though the precise mode of human acquisition is thought to be inhalational
Diagnosis is confirmed by culture from blood, skin, bone marrow or lymph node, with the fungus showing characteristic fission-yeast morphology and a diffusible red pigment in culture
It closely mimics disseminated tuberculosis, histoplasmosis and cryptococcosis, so a high index of suspicion is essential in HIV-positive travellers or residents from endemic areas
Treatment follows an induction phase with amphotericin-based therapy followed by azole consolidation and, in HIV, secondary prophylaxis until immune reconstitution
reference.pathophysiology: Talaromyces marneffei is inhaled as conidia that convert to a pathogenic yeast-like form dividing by fission at body temperature. In hosts with intact cell-mediated immunity infection is usually contained, but in advanced HIV or other T-cell deficiency the organism proliferates within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. Haematogenous dissemination follows, seeding skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen and lymph nodes, producing a granulomatous, suppurative or necrotising reaction depending on immune status. Uncontrolled fungaemia leads to sepsis and multiorgan involvement.
additionalInvestigations: Fungal culture of blood, skin lesion, bone marrow or lymph node aspirate
Microscopy of skin scrapings or tissue for intracellular fission yeasts
HIV testing and CD4 count in all suspected cases
Antigen-based assays where available for earlier diagnosis
Assessment for concurrent opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis
redFlags: Disseminated disease with sepsis and multiorgan involvement
Advanced HIV with very low CD4 count and high fungal burden
Delayed diagnosis due to mimicry of tuberculosis, which markedly increases mortality
reference.prognosis: Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is almost uniformly fatal, but early antifungal induction and consolidation with antiretroviral therapy and secondary prophylaxis achieve good outcomes; mortality remains high when diagnosis is delayed or the patient presents with sepsis.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as tuberculosis and delaying antifungal therapy
Stopping antifungals or secondary prophylaxis prematurely before immune reconstitution
Overlooking the diagnosis in HIV patients with relevant travel or residence history
Attributing umbilicated skin lesions solely to molluscum contagiosum
management: Treat disseminated disease with induction antifungal therapy using liposomal amphotericin B
Follow induction with consolidation itraconazole therapy, with voriconazole as an alternative
Continue secondary antifungal prophylaxis with itraconazole until immune reconstitution on antiretroviral therapy
Initiate or optimise antiretroviral therapy in HIV-associated disease, timing it to reduce immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome
Provide supportive care for sepsis, anaemia and organ dysfunction during the acute illness
Screen for and manage concurrent opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis
Monitor CD4 count and treatment response, escalating for severe sepsis or multiorgan involvement
Coordinate care between infectious diseases and HIV services
